overview: This file contains a despatch from the American consul at Dairen reporting that the Marine Bureau of the Imperial Japanese Kwantung Government established a government-operated vessel-fumigation service at Dairen and Port Arthur on July 1, 1931, and began issuing fumigation certificates. It also describes limited after-sunset quarantine inspections and provides fee schedules for ordinary and special sulphur fumigation, rodent and vermin destruction, and night inspections, with special procedures intended chiefly for vessels bound for the United States and its possessions. The consul requests that the information be shared with American public-health and naval-intelligence authorities, with copies sent to officials in Manila and Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Despatch on fumigation service and night quarantine inspection at Dairen and Port Arthur
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the establishment of a government vessel-fumigation service and after-sunset quarantine inspections at Dairen and Port Arthur, together with the applicable fees.
subfiles.summary: Langdon reports that on July 1, 1931, the Marine Bureau of the Imperial Japanese Kwantung Government assumed responsibility for fumigating vessels at Dairen and Port Arthur and began issuing fumigation certificates. The despatch lists graduated fees based on vessel tonnage for ordinary hold fumigation and special fumigation of all compartments, the latter chiefly intended for vessels bound for the United States and its possessions. It also gives separate night-quarantine inspection fees for passenger ships and other vessels. Langdon asks the Department of State to transmit the information to the United States Public Health Service and the Navy Department’s Office of Naval Intelligence, while copies are distributed to Manila and Tokyo.

interest: The despatch provides unusually concrete evidence of how Japanese colonial authorities administered maritime sanitation in the Kwantung Leased Territory, including an exact fee structure differentiated by ship size and level of fumigation. Its reference to special whole-vessel fumigation for ships bound to the United States and its possessions illustrates how American sanitary requirements shaped practices in an East Asian port. The requested circulation to public-health, customs, diplomatic, and naval-intelligence offices also shows the overlap among disease control, shipping regulation, colonial administration, and strategic information gathering.
